items.prompt: In test-driven development, what is the first step of each cycle?

options.label: Write a failing automated test
Run a manual check of the running app
Refactor the existing code to be cleaner
Write the production code for the feature

rubric: TDD starts with a failing test (red) before any production code.
Writing code first is the classic non-TDD order.

items.prompt: What does the "green" step in red-green-refactor mean?

options.label: All tests pass
Code is live
A new test added
Code is cleaned up

rubric: Green means the tests pass.
Cleaning up is refactor; writing a new test is red.

items.prompt: In red-green-refactor, which step comes third?

options.label: Refactor
Red
Green
Deploy

rubric: The order is red, green, refactor.
Red and green come before refactor.

items.prompt: What does the "red" state mean in the TDD cycle?

options.label: The code has a syntax error
The build is slow
A test is failing
The code needs refactoring

rubric: Red means a newly written test fails.
It is not about general errors or slowness.

items.prompt: Which is another common name for TDD?

options.label: Test-last development
Test-first development
Waterfall testing
Manual regression testing

rubric: TDD is also called test-first development.
Test-last is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which of these are steps of the red-green-refactor cycle? Select all that apply.

options.label: Write a failing test
Delete all tests after passing
Make the test pass
Clean up the code while tests stay green

rubric: The cycle is: failing test, make it pass, refactor.
Deleting tests defeats the safety net.

items.prompt: A new developer joins a team that uses TDD. She is asked to add a function `is_even(n)`. She asks what to do first, before writing any code for the function.

options.label: Refactor the module so the function fits in
Write a docstring listing inputs and outputs
Write a test that calls `is_even` and fails
Write the simplest working `is_even`, then test it

rubric: The first step is a failing test.
Writing the function first, even a simple one, breaks test-first order, since the test must come before the code.

items.prompt: Why do we run a new test and see it fail before writing the code?

options.label: It lets us skip the refactor step once the test passes
It makes the code we write afterwards run faster
It proves the feature is already correctly built
It shows the test can detect missing behaviour

rubric: A failing test confirms it actually checks something.
A test that never failed might pass for the wrong reason.

items.prompt: In the green step, what is the right goal when writing code?

options.label: Optimise the code for speed before the test passes
Write the simplest code that makes the test pass
Add features the tests do not ask for yet, to save time
Build the full final design now so no rework is needed

rubric: Green aims for the simplest passing code.
Over-building goes beyond what tests require.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the refactor step?

options.label: Skip writing tests so the work finishes sooner
Improve code structure without changing behaviour
Add the next piece of new behaviour to the code
Rewrite failing tests so that they all pass again

rubric: Refactoring improves structure while behaviour stays the same.
Adding behaviour needs a new failing test.

items.prompt: How big should each TDD cycle be?

options.label: Small, adding one tiny behaviour at a time
Medium, finishing one whole function per cycle
Sized to the sprint, one user story per cycle
Large, covering a whole feature before refactoring

rubric: TDD works in small increments.
Large steps make failures hard to locate.

items.prompt: How does TDD help when you later change the code?

options.label: Failing tests quickly show a change broke behaviour
Tests rewrite the broken code to match the new change
Tests prove the new code has no bugs, so no one needs to rerun them
Tests lock the code, so changes need the tests rewritten first

rubric: The suite acts as a safety net that flags regressions.
Tests do not edit or block code.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe TDD? Select all that apply.

options.label: A new test should pass the first time it runs, which proves it checks the right thing
Refactoring happens when tests are passing
Tests are written before the code they check
Each cycle adds the full feature, and tests are written once the code is done

items.prompt: A developer wrote a test for `add(2, 3)` expecting 5. She runs it before writing `add`, and it fails with an error that the function does not exist. A teammate asks if that counts as the red step.

options.label: Yes, the test fails, so it is red
No, red needs the code finished first
Yes, but only after she refactors
No, red only counts when a test passes

rubric: A failing test, even from a missing function, is red.
Red is about failure, not finished code.

items.prompt: Why does TDD have you write a test before the production code?

options.label: It guarantees the code has no bugs, because every possible input is tested first
It lets testers work apart from developers, who then need not know the requirements
It removes the need to run tests later, because the early test covers the whole program
It makes you state the expected behavior first, so the code has a clear target

rubric: Writing the test first defines the expected behavior before any code exists.
Distractors treat TDD as a guarantee of bug-free code or as a replacement for later testing.

items.prompt: In red-green-refactor, what do you do in the green step?

options.label: List every edge case you can think of and write tests for all of them first
Remove the failing test once you understand why it is red, then move on
Write just enough code to make the one failing test pass, nothing more
Redesign the whole module so it stays clean and flexible for future features

rubric: Green means the simplest code that passes the current failing test.
Distractors confuse green with refactoring, with up-front test planning, or with deleting tests.

items.prompt: Why should you run a new test and watch it fail before writing the code?

options.label: It shows the test can detect missing behavior, so a later pass actually means something
It proves the test framework is installed, which is the main purpose of the red step
It lets you estimate how long the code will take, based on how many assertions fail
It records the bug for a report, since red tests are required before any merge

rubric: Seeing red confirms the test is capable of failing, so it is a meaningful check.
Distractors give unrelated purposes such as setup checking or estimating.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the refactor step?

options.label: Rewriting the tests so they match whatever the code currently happens to output
Improving the code's structure while its behavior stays the same and tests stay green
Adding a new feature while the tests are red, then updating the whole suite once the feature works
Optimizing for speed first, then checking afterward whether the existing behavior has changed

rubric: Refactoring changes structure, not behavior, and is protected by passing tests.
Distractors mix in feature work, test rewriting, or unchecked changes.

items.prompt: You write a new test for a feature and it passes on its first run, before you write any new code. What does this most likely mean?

options.label: The code is finished, since a first-run pass shows the design is already correct
The behavior may already exist, or the test is not checking anything that could fail
The test is ideal, because passing tests are the main goal of the red step
The test framework is broken, because new tests must always fail by definition

rubric: An immediate pass means the behavior already exists or the test is too weak.
Distractors treat the pass as proof of correctness or blame the framework.

items.prompt: Which are benefits of working in small red-green-refactor cycles? Select all that apply.

options.label: The suite grows with the code, so you can refactor with confidence
Design decisions are postponed until the whole feature is coded
A failing test points to the few lines changed most recently
Fewer tests are needed, since each cycle replaces the previous test
Each step ends in a working state you can return to

rubric: Small cycles localize failures, build a safety net, and keep a working state.
Distractors claim postponed design or that tests are replaced each cycle.

items.prompt: A developer writes the test `isLeapYear(2024) == true`. To make it pass she writes `return true`. A teammate calls this cheating. Which explanation best shows why it is acceptable in TDD?

options.label: It is wrong, because green code has to implement the full general leap-year rule before the test can pass
It is fine, because refactoring will later generalise the constant, so more tests are not needed
It is a valid small step to green, and later tests like 1900 being false will force a real rule
It is a finished solution, because passing the tests that exist now is the main requirement of TDD

rubric: A hardcoded value is a valid small step; more tests then drive the general rule.
Distractors treat the shortcut as final or forbid it outright.

items.prompt: Tests for `fizzbuzz(1)` and `fizzbuzz(2)` pass. The next requirement is that multiples of 3 return "Fizz". What is the next TDD step?

options.label: Write a failing test expecting `fizzbuzz(3)` to return "Fizz" and run it
Write code for Fizz, Buzz and FizzBuzz together, then test all three rules
Refactor `fizzbuzz` into several helper functions before adding behavior
Add the multiple-of-3 branch to `fizzbuzz`, then write its test afterward

rubric: The next cycle starts with a new failing test for the new behavior.
Distractors write code before the test or batch several rules together.

items.prompt: All tests pass. You notice `invoiceTotal` and `quoteTotal` both contain the line `price * qty * 1.2`. What is the best next step?

options.label: Change the rate in one function to see which tests fail first
Leave it alone, because refactoring is only allowed while a test is failing
Extract the helper and skip rerunning tests, since behavior is unchanged by design
Extract the shared calculation into one helper, then rerun the tests

rubric: Remove duplication in the refactor step, then rerun tests to confirm behavior is unchanged.
Distractors refactor on red, skip verification, or change behavior.

items.prompt: You refactor a function and two previously passing tests now fail. What should you do?

options.label: Undo the refactoring step to return to green, then retry in a smaller change
Delete the two tests, since refactoring should not need them
Edit the failing tests until they match the new output, then continue
Keep refactoring further, since the tests will probably pass once the cleanup is done

rubric: Refactoring must keep tests green, so revert and take a smaller step.
Distractors alter or remove tests, or push on while red.

items.prompt: You start building `cartTotal(items)` with no code yet. Which is the best first test to write?

options.label: `cartTotal(null)` raises a custom error with a localized message
`cartTotal` finishes in under one millisecond for very large carts
`cartTotal` of 100 mixed items with a coupon and tax gives the exact total
`cartTotal([])` returns 0

rubric: Start with the simplest case, which leads to a tiny first step.
Distractors are complex or non-functional cases that demand too much at once.

items.prompt: To pass `add(2, 3) == 5` you wrote `return 5`. Which test should you add next to force a real implementation?
rubric: Only a test with a different expected result breaks the hardcoded 5.
The other tests all expect 5 and would pass with the hardcoded value.

items.prompt: A bug report says a 10% coupon is applied twice on orders over 100. Which actions follow TDD? Select all that apply.

options.label: Change only the code needed to make that test pass
Run the full suite after the fix to check nothing else broke
Write a failing test that reproduces the double discount
Fix the code first, then write a test to confirm it afterward
Delete older discount tests that fail, since they predate the bug

rubric: Reproduce the bug with a failing test, make the minimal fix, and run the whole suite.
Distractors fix before testing or remove inconvenient tests.

items.prompt: `wordCount` is implemented as `return len(text.split(" "))` and passes the test for "hi there" returning 2. You add the test `wordCount("") == 0`; it fails because the function returns 1. What is the best change in the green step?

options.label: Change the new test to expect 1, since `split` returns one item for an empty string
Replace the function body with `return 0`, then rerun the tests
Rewrite it with a regex tokenizer and helper classes to handle all possible input
Add `if text == "": return 0` before the existing line, then rerun all tests

rubric: A small change fixes the new test while keeping the earlier test passing.
Distractors break the old test, weaken the new test, or overbuild beyond what the test needs.

items.prompt: You are building `is_leap_year(year)` with TDD. Your first test, `is_leap_year(2024) == True`, is passing after you returned `year % 4 == 0`. What should you do next?

options.label: Refactor the function into a class with helper methods before adding any more tests, so the design is clean first
Write tests for every year from 1 to 3000 in one go, then write the code that makes them all pass
Add the full century rule to the code now, since you know it, then write tests for it afterwards
Write a failing test such as `is_leap_year(1900) == False`, then change the code to pass it

rubric: Each new behaviour starts with a failing test; 1900 exposes the missing century rule.
Coding ahead of tests or writing huge test batches breaks the small red-green cycle.

items.prompt: You wrote a test `add(2, 3) == 5` for a function `add` that does not exist yet. You run it. What is the correct outcome to expect and do?

options.label: It passes because the assertion is mathematically true; move on to the next test
It fails; delete the test because a missing function means the test is invalid
It fails (error that `add` is undefined); write the simplest code to make it pass
It fails; write a complete calculator module with every operation so it never fails again

rubric: Red phase: a failing test confirms the test can fail; then write minimal code.
Overbuilding a calculator skips the incremental approach.

items.prompt: Your test `price_with_tax(100, 0.2) == 120` is red. The simplest code to turn it green is `return 120`. You then add a second test `price_with_tax(50, 0.1) == 55`. What is the best next code step?

options.label: Generalise to `return price * (1 + rate)` so both tests pass
Add an `if` branch for each input pair so both tests pass
Leave the code and delete the second test since 120 already passes
Rewrite the whole module with a tax strategy class for future rates

rubric: A second example triangulates and drives the general formula.
Branch-per-case or speculative design doesn't generalise or follows no test need.

items.prompt: All tests are green. The function contains the same 4-line discount calculation copied in two places. Following red-green-refactor, what do you do?

options.label: Write a failing test for the duplication, then change behaviour to pass it
Leave the duplication until the feature is done, then clean up
Extract the lines and tweak the discount rules too, then rerun the tests
Extract the duplicated lines into one function and rerun the tests

rubric: Refactoring happens on green, preserves behaviour, and is verified by rerunning tests.
Mixing in behaviour changes during refactoring breaks the discipline.

items.prompt: You are TDD-ing `parse_age(text)`, which should return an int and raise `ValueError` for non-numeric text. The int case already passes. Which test do you write next?

options.label: A test that calls `parse_age("42")` again with a different variable name
Production code that raises `ValueError`, with a test added afterwards
A test of the Python `int` built-in to confirm it rejects letters
A test asserting `parse_age("abc")` raises `ValueError`, run to see it fail

rubric: The next required behaviour gets a failing test first.
Repeating a passing case adds no information; testing the library is out of scope.

items.prompt: You are about to start a TDD cycle for a `Stack.pop()` method that should return the last pushed item. Which actions fit the red-green-refactor cycle? Select all that apply.

options.label: After it passes, rename variables and tidy code while keeping tests green
Write a test that pushes 1 and 2 and expects `pop()` to return 2, and watch it fail
Implement `pop()`, `peek()` and `size()` fully before running any test, since they share the same internal list
Once the `pop()` test is green, add a test-less `peek()` method because it is trivial and unlikely to break

items.prompt: You are adding a `fizzbuzz(n)` function with TDD. Existing green tests cover `fizzbuzz(1) == "1"` and `fizzbuzz(3) == "Fizz"`. The code is `if n % 3 == 0: return "Fizz"; return str(n)`. What is the next step?

options.label: Refactor the function into a lookup table of divisors before any new test
Write a failing test for `fizzbuzz(5) == "Buzz"` and then add the minimal code
Add the `Buzz` and `FizzBuzz` branches now, since the rules are known
Write the test for `fizzbuzz(15)` and the code for `fizzbuzz(5)` together

rubric: Next behaviour gets one failing test, then minimal code.
Writing ahead of tests or jumping to a bigger case skips small steps.

items.prompt: A developer writes a test and code together, then runs the test, which passes immediately. Later the test is found to pass even when the function returns a hard-coded wrong value. Which TDD step would most likely have exposed this?

options.label: Watching the test fail before writing the code, proving the assertion can detect missing behaviour
Running the green step again after refactoring, which confirms the code still passes every existing test
Writing the simplest code that passes, so that the hard-coded value shows up as a design smell right away
Adding a second test for the same function after the code is done, so both tests confirm the same behaviour

rubric: The red step verifies the test can fail for the right reason.
The other options don't check the test's sensitivity.

items.prompt: A team's TDD suite breaks in 30 places whenever they refactor internals, though behaviour is unchanged. Tests assert exact private method calls via mocks. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Tests are coupled to implementation details, not observable behaviour
Refactoring is happening without a matching set of new tests for each moved method
Too few mocks are used, so the tests cannot isolate each unit from its collaborators
The tests were written before the code, so they lock in a design that was guessed early

rubric: Asserting internal calls couples tests to structure, so refactors break them.
Test-first is not the cause, and more mocks worsen the coupling.

items.prompt: A developer's tests for a `Cart.total()` pass one at a time but the full suite fails randomly. Each test adds items to a shared module-level `cart` object. What is the likely root cause?

options.label: Shared mutable state lets tests affect each other depending on run order
The production code needs more refactoring to become deterministic
The tests are too small and should be merged into one large test
The failing tests should be deleted since they pass individually

rubric: Shared state creates order dependence; tests need fresh setup.
Merging tests or deleting them hides the isolation problem.

items.prompt: In a TDD session you write a test, make it pass with the simplest code, and then every next test also passes instantly without any code change. What does this most likely indicate?

options.label: The new tests repeat behaviour already covered, so they add little design pressure
The refactoring step was skipped, so the design must be cleaned up before any further tests can fail
The feature is finished, so the design cannot be improved and further tests are unnecessary
The tests are too strict and should be loosened so that they sometimes fail again

rubric: Instantly green tests suggest redundancy or an earlier over-generalised step.
Skipped refactoring or strictness does not explain it.

items.prompt: You must test `send_receipt(order)` which calls a real email server. Tests are slow and flaky. Which analysis best fits a TDD approach?

options.label: Hide the email behind an interface and use a fake in tests, since the server causes the slowness
Replace every collaborator in the codebase with a mock so that no production code runs in any test
Skip unit tests for this function because TDD only suits pure logic, and rely on manual checks
Keep the real server but add retries and longer timeouts so that the flaky tests eventually pass

rubric: Isolating the external dependency fixes the cause and improves design.
Retries mask flakiness; mocking everything removes test value.

items.prompt: A TDD test for `apply_discount(total, code)` fails after a refactor even though no behaviour was intended to change. Which findings would explain it? Select all that apply.

options.label: The refactor accidentally altered rounding in the calculation
The test failed because it was written before the code
The refactor was done while a different test was still red
The test asserts on an internal helper's name that was renamed

rubric: Behaviour change, implementation coupling and refactoring on red all explain failures.
Writing the test first is not a cause of later failure.

items.prompt: A developer TDDs a `slugify(title)` function. Tests: `"Hello World"` gives `"hello-world"`; `"A B"` gives `"a-b"`. Code: `title.lower().replace(" ", "-")`. A bug report shows `"Hello  World"` (two spaces) gives `"hello--world"`. What does this reveal?

options.label: The tests missed an edge case, so reproduce it in a failing test before fixing
The code is the only problem, so fix it first and add a test afterward to confirm the fix
The existing tests are wrong, so replace them with one broad test covering every input
TDD failed as a method here, so write the tests after the code from now on

rubric: Missed edge case: reproduce with a failing test, then fix.
Abandoning TDD or fixing without a test loses regression protection.

items.prompt: A developer writes a new test for a discount rule before touching production code, runs it, and it passes immediately. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: The discount rule is too simple to need a failing test first, so a pass is fine
The test never exercises the new behaviour, or the behaviour already exists
The production code is faster than expected, so it needs no change for this rule
The test runner cached the previous green result and skipped running the new test

rubric: A test that passes without new code gives no evidence it can detect the missing behaviour, so it is vacuous or redundant.
Distractors treat an unexpected green as a harmless success.

items.prompt: A team's suite fails on nearly every internal refactor even though no observable behaviour changes. Most tests mock each collaborator and verify the exact calls made between internal classes. What is the root cause?

options.label: The team refactors too often and should batch changes into larger rewrites
The tests are coupled to the implementation structure instead of observable behaviour
The suite has too few tests, so the refactors are not covered well enough
The mocking library is out of date and reports false failures whenever classes are renamed or moved

rubric: Interaction-verifying tests pin the internal design, so structural changes break them without any behaviour change.
Distractors blame the quantity of tests or tooling rather than the coupling.

items.prompt: After the first test `add(2, 2) == 4`, a developer writes `return 4`. Why is the next step to add a test such as `add(3, 5) == 8`?

options.label: To increase the coverage percentage of the `add` function
To force the hardcoded value to be generalised into real logic
To check that the first test still passes after the change
To confirm the compiler accepts the new function signature

rubric: Triangulation adds a case the fake implementation cannot satisfy, driving the general solution.
Coverage is already complete for the one line, so that distractor misreads the purpose.

items.prompt: In the red step, a new test fails with a `NullPointerException` thrown in test setup because a fixture was not built. The developer proceeds to write production code. What is the main problem with this?

options.label: The test never reached its assertion, so a later green would not prove the behaviour
The setup failure shows the production code already contains a defect that must be fixed first
An exception counts as a valid red only when the production class under test throws it
Fixtures should be created by production code, so the test should not build its own objects

rubric: Red must be for the intended reason; otherwise the test may later pass or fail for reasons unrelated to the behaviour.
Distractors misattribute the failure to production code or ban exceptions outright.

items.prompt: Two teams practise TDD on an order service. Team A asserts on returned totals and stored state. Team B asserts that `PriceCalculator.apply` and `TaxClient.fetch` were each called once with specific arguments. Extracting a new class inside the service will most likely affect which team, and why?

options.label: Both equally, because every test depends on the class structure
Team B, because its assertions encode which collaborators talk to each other
Neither team, because extracting a class never changes any test result
Team A, because state assertions depend on how the class is split

rubric: Interaction assertions fix the collaboration structure, so restructuring breaks them.
State-based tests survive when observable results are unchanged.

items.prompt: A team's suite is green, but reviewers suspect the refactor step is being skipped. Which observations support that suspicion? Select all that apply.

options.label: Production code contains `if (input == 42)` branches that exist only to satisfy individual tests
The same validation logic is copied into several classes while all tests pass
The suite takes longer to run than it did last month
Test names describe behaviours instead of method names

rubric: Test-specific special cases and duplicated logic are residue that the refactor step should remove.
Run time and test naming are unrelated to skipped refactoring.

items.prompt: A developer writes eight tests for a parser, then spends two hours writing the whole implementation. Six tests fail, and tracing them reveals three separate defects interacting. A colleague says this is not really TDD. Which aspect of the practice was broken, and what does it explain?

options.label: The parser should have been tested only at the end-to-end level, since unit tests cannot expose interacting defects
Refactoring was done too early in the cycle, which hid the source of the defects from the tests
Tests were written before the code, which makes the resulting failures harder to read and trace
Cycles were too large, so a failure could not be tied to the last small change

rubric: TDD relies on one small red-green step at a time so any failure points at the latest change.
Writing tests first is not the problem; the batch size is.

items.prompt: You must fix a defect in a 2,000-line untested legacy billing function before a release in two days. Criteria: protect existing behaviour, keep the change small, and avoid a rewrite. Which approach best fits?

options.label: Add unit tests only for new code in other modules, then leave the legacy billing function untouched and unpatched
Rewrite the whole function through strict TDD so that every billing rule is reimplemented and covered by tests
Patch the defect directly and rely on manual regression testing of the main billing flows, since no tests exist yet
Write a failing test for the defect plus characterization tests around the touched path, then fix

rubric: Characterization tests pin current behaviour around the change while a failing test proves the fix.
A rewrite violates the small-change criterion; untested patching ignores protecting behaviour.

items.prompt: A team must integrate an unfamiliar third-party payments API whose behaviour is poorly documented. Criteria: learn quickly, then end with a well-tested design. Which plan is the best trade-off?

options.label: Write a throwaway spike to learn the API, discard it, then TDD the real code
Skip tests for the integration entirely because the vendor tests their API
Keep the spike as production code and add tests afterwards to reach full coverage
Strictly TDD every exploratory call from the first minute, even before knowing the responses

rubric: A discarded spike answers the unknowns cheaply, and then test-first builds a clean tested design.
Keeping spike code undermines the tested-design criterion.

items.prompt: A manager proposes a mandatory 100% line-coverage gate as proof that the team practises TDD. Which critique is strongest?

options.label: A 100% target is too low, so a gate on branch coverage should replace it as proof of TDD
Coverage only matters for legacy code, because test-first code is covered by construction
Coverage cannot be measured accurately for code written test-first, so the gate is unreliable
Coverage shows lines executed, not behaviour asserted, and gates invite weak tests

rubric: Coverage measures execution, not verification, and targets encourage assertion-free tests.
Other options misstate what coverage can show or what it is for.

items.prompt: Code applies a late fee when an invoice is more than 30 days old, using the system clock. Criteria: deterministic tests, fast runs, and minimal production changes. Which approach is best?

options.label: Inject a clock the code reads from, and have tests supply fixed dates
Test only invoices dated far in the past so the boundary never matters
Change the machine clock before each test run and restore it afterwards
Use `sleep` in tests until real time passes the 30-day boundary

rubric: An injected clock gives deterministic, fast tests with a small seam in the code.
Sleeping or altering the system clock is slow or fragile, and skipping the boundary leaves the rule untested.

items.prompt: A single test named `testCheckout` creates a cart, applies a coupon, charges a card, sends an email and asserts on eight things. Criteria: failure localisation and readable intent. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Acceptable, because a single test per feature keeps the suite small
Remove the assertions on the email and coupon and keep the card assertion only
Split it into focused tests, each with one reason to fail and a behaviour-based name
Keep it and add comments next to each assertion to explain the failures

rubric: Focused tests localise failures and document behaviour.
Comments or deleting checks neither fix localisation nor preserve coverage.

items.prompt: During a refactor, a team reviews its tests against the criteria of low maintenance cost and confidence in behaviour. Which tests are justified candidates for deletion or rewrite? Select all that apply.

options.label: A test duplicating another test's exact scenario and assertions at the same level
A slow end-to-end test of checkout that is the only check that payment, stock and email services work together
A test covering a rarely used but specified refund rule through the public API
A test that calls a private helper through reflection and asserts its internal return value

rubric: Implementation-coupled and exact duplicate tests add cost without new confidence.
The refund rule test protects specified behaviour, so it should stay.

items.prompt: A team builds a repository class that runs SQL queries. Criteria: fast feedback during the TDD loop, but also confidence that the real queries work. Developers are debating how to test it. Which strategy best meets both criteria?

options.label: Test only through the UI, so every query is exercised by real user flows and skip repository-level tests
Test against a real, disposable database in small fast tests, keeping business logic tests free of it
Mock the database driver and verify the exact SQL strings sent, so each test runs in memory with no setup
Run every test against a shared staging database, so the queries meet the same data and engine as production

rubric: Real queries need a real engine, and disposable instances keep loops fast while logic tests stay isolated.
Mocking SQL strings proves nothing about query correctness; a shared staging database is slow and flaky.

items.prompt: A team refactors a pricing module often, splitting and merging internal classes. They want tests that stay green through such restructuring but still catch behavioural regressions. Which test strategy best fits these criteria?

options.label: Rely solely on end-to-end UI tests, so that no test knows anything about how the code is structured inside
Test through the module's public interface with real internal collaborators, using fakes only at external boundaries
Write one test per private method, so each internal unit has direct coverage however the classes are arranged
Mock every collaborator and verify each call, so each class is isolated and any internal change is flagged at once

rubric: Behaviour-level tests through the public interface survive internal refactoring while still detecting regressions.
Per-class mocks and private-method tests couple tests to structure, so they break on harmless restructuring.

items.prompt: A manager says: 'Our coverage is 96%, so the team is clearly doing TDD properly.' Which critique of this claim is strongest?

options.label: Coverage is a lagging number that tests written after the code can also reach, so it cannot show tests drove the design
Coverage proves TDD only when branch coverage is also reported, because line coverage alone hides the test ordering
Coverage counts only integration tests, so it says nothing about whether unit tests were written before the code
Coverage above 90% is impossible under strict TDD, because tests written first always leave some branches unexecuted

rubric: Coverage measures what executed, not the order in which tests and code were written.
Distractors invent false limits on coverage or confuse what the metric counts.

items.prompt: Developers commit several times an hour, but the suite takes 14 minutes, mostly from database-backed tests of pure business rules. Which is the most serious risk to the TDD workflow?

options.label: The database will be overloaded, which is the main reason test-first work cannot be repeated by teammates
Tests will be too precise, which makes refactoring riskier because every behaviour is pinned down in detail
Business rules will become unreachable by tests, because pure logic cannot be verified without a database
Developers will batch many changes per run, which enlarges steps and weakens the quick red-green feedback

rubric: Slow feedback pushes people into big steps, which erodes the small-cycle discipline TDD depends on.
Other options misattribute the problem to precision, load, or testability of pure logic.

items.prompt: While test-driving a date-range overlap function, a developer used the obvious implementation twice, and both times a hidden edge case broke a later test. Judged on feedback speed and risk, what is the best next move?

options.label: Keep the obvious implementation but write every remaining test up front, so all edge cases are known before coding
Shrink the steps: fake it with a constant, then triangulate with a second example to force the general rule out
Skip the red step for edge cases, since the logic is understood and a failing test adds no new information
Write the implementation first and add tests afterward, documenting whatever the code already does for each case

rubric: Repeated surprises signal that steps are too large; fake-it and triangulation shrink them.
Writing all tests up front, skipping red, or going test-after discards the incremental feedback that exposes edge cases.

items.prompt: A team must learn an undocumented vendor SDK's behaviour, and the production integration must end up well tested. Judged on learning speed and final test quality, which approach is best?

options.label: Explore in a throwaway spike without tests, discard it, then test-drive the real code using what was learned
Test-drive the SDK calls from the first line, so every experiment is a failing test that specifies SDK behaviour in advance
Write the whole integration untested and ship it once it works, adding tests only if users later report defects
Mock the whole SDK from its documentation and test-drive against the mock, so real behaviour never needs exploring

rubric: A discarded spike answers questions cheaply; then TDD builds the real design with known facts.
Mocking undocumented behaviour encodes guesses, and shipping untested code fails the quality criterion.

items.prompt: A suite built with heavy mocking breaks whenever internals are refactored, even though behaviour is unchanged. Which are valid criticisms of this testing style? Select all that apply.

options.label: Tests verify interaction sequences rather than outcomes, which couples them to the implementation
Mocks of types the team does not own can hide real contract changes in those dependencies
Mocks run slower than real objects, which is the actual cause of the breakage on refactoring
Stubbing internal collaborators' return values duplicates their logic in setup, so changes ripple through many tests
Mocks make it impossible for any test to fail first, so the red step cannot be performed

rubric: Interaction verification, unowned-type mocks and duplicated stub logic are real weaknesses of over-mocking.
Speed is not the cause of refactoring breakage, and mocked tests can still fail first.

items.prompt: A team test-drove a shipping-cost module for a year. A mutation run shows 30% of mutants survive, mostly boundary changes such as `>=` to `>` on weight thresholds. Time is limited and the thresholds directly affect revenue. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Treat the score as meaningless, since test-first code cannot have surviving mutants and the tool must be misconfigured
Add boundary tests for the costliest thresholds, and set aside equivalent or low-risk mutants rather than chase 100%
Delete code paths with surviving mutants, since logic no test pins down is unused and therefore safe to remove
Rewrite the module test-after with a 100% line coverage target, since that guarantees every mutant will be killed

rubric: Surviving boundary mutants reveal missing triangulation; prioritising by risk fits the time and revenue criteria.
Other options deny the evidence, delete live code, or wrongly equate line coverage with killing mutants.

items.prompt: Design the first failing test for a rate limiter allowing 3 requests per 10-second window. Constraints: deterministic, runs in milliseconds, and the limiter's public behaviour is not changed for production. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Patch the system clock globally and assert the limiter's internal counter equals one after a single request is made
Call the real limiter four times with real sleeps between runs, then confirm the window resets after ten seconds elapse
Use real time and assert the limiter's internal map holds three entries after three requests are sent in a loop
Construct the limiter with a controllable clock, make three requests at t=0, and assert a fourth at t=0 is rejected

rubric: An injected clock gives determinism and speed, and the assertion checks observable behaviour at the limit.
Sleeps are slow, and asserting internal state or using real time is brittle and implementation-coupled.

items.prompt: A test for `isExpired(token)` fails intermittently near midnight because it reads the system clock. Constraints: production callers stay unchanged, the test is deterministic, and no sleeping is allowed. Which change meets all of them?

options.label: Make the test sleep until just after midnight, so that both setup and assertion see the same calendar date
Wrap the assertion in a retry loop of up to five attempts, so a failure near midnight eventually passes on a retry
Add an optional clock parameter defaulting to the system clock, and have the test pass a fixed clock
Require every caller to pass the current time explicitly, changing all call sites so no default clock remains

rubric: A defaulted, injectable clock keeps callers unchanged and makes the test deterministic.
Retries and sleeps keep nondeterminism, and forcing all callers to change violates the constraint.

items.prompt: You must add a discount rule to a 400-line untested `calculateInvoice` function. Constraints: no behaviour change beyond the new rule, and every step small and reversible. Which plan meets them?

options.label: Rewrite the function from scratch test-first, then compare its output against the old version on production traffic after release
Write the failing discount test and pass it with an inline edit to the existing function, then refactor later once the release is out
Pin current behaviour with characterization tests, then test-drive the discount and refactor under that net
Extract every helper in one large commit and unit test each afterward, then add the discount rule on top of the new structure

rubric: Characterization tests create a safety net so the new rule and refactoring proceed in small safe steps.
Rewriting, big-bang extraction, or inline edits without a net risk unintended behaviour changes.

items.prompt: A team's written routine is: 1) write a test, 2) write the simplest code that passes it, 3) refactor with tests green, 4) commit. Which essential element does this proposed design omit?

options.label: Running the full end-to-end suite after every single line edit, so that any regression is never more than a few seconds old
Adding a second test for every behaviour immediately, so that each feature has duplicate coverage from the outset of work
Running the new test before the code to see it fail for the expected reason, proving it can detect the gap
Writing a full design document before the first test, so that the tests have a fixed and complete target to verify

rubric: Seeing the test fail for the right reason shows the test can detect missing behaviour; without it a test may pass vacuously.
Other options add heavy process that TDD does not require.

items.prompt: Feature: customers can cancel an order. Constraints: the team wants proof the feature works end to end, while the internal design emerges from small units. Which plan meets both?

options.label: Write a failing acceptance test for cancellation, then drive the units with small red-green-refactor cycles until it passes
Write only one acceptance test and implement everything in one step, since unit cycles would duplicate its coverage
Write all unit tests for every planned class first, then write acceptance tests once the last class is finished
Write unit tests per class from design diagrams, and treat a manual walkthrough as the end-to-end proof

rubric: The double loop gives end-to-end proof from the outer test and emergent design from inner unit cycles.
Other plans delay end-to-end proof, drop the unit cycles, or replace automated proof with manual checks.

items.prompt: Design a test-first approach for a payment gateway integration. Constraints: unit tests are fast and deterministic, the design is driven test-first, and changes to the real gateway's contract are still detected. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: A small contract test suite run against the gateway sandbox on a separate schedule from the unit tests
Contract tests that also run against the fake, so the fake and real adapter meet the same expectations
Mocks of the app's own internal classes that verify call order for every payment flow in detail
Calls to the live gateway inside every unit test, so that behaviour under test is always the real behaviour
A thin adapter interface owned by the app, with a fake implementation used in test-driven unit tests

rubric: An owned adapter with a fake keeps units fast; sandbox contract tests catch drift; running them on the fake keeps it honest.
Live calls in unit tests break speed and determinism, and internal-class mocks add coupling without detecting contract changes.

items.prompt: A team will test-drive a parser for a config format whose dozen rules arrive over several weeks. Constraints: adding a rule must be cheap, tests must stay readable, and the design must emerge incrementally. Which plan best meets all three?

options.label: Write the complete parser from the spec first, then generate one large test that combines inputs from every rule
Test only the parsed object for one huge realistic file, since small inputs do not reflect real usage
Mock the tokenizer in every test and verify the call sequence, so each rule's tests stay independent
Keep a table of input and expected result, add one row per rule as a failing case, make it pass, and refactor

rubric: A growing example table makes each new rule a cheap, readable red-green-refactor cycle that lets the design emerge.
Parser-first code, one huge file, or call-sequence mocks fail the incremental, readable, or cheap-to-extend constraints.
